claims.text: The homogenized and annealed HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions govern the elevated-temperature stress–strain behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Sluggish diffusion governs the elevated-temperature stress–strain behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions and sluggish diffusion govern the thermal expansion of HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions and sluggish diffusion govern the elevated-temperature elastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
The constituent elements of HfNbTaTiZr have a significant atomic-size mismatch that produces lattice distortions.
Lattice distortions reduce dislocation mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
Sluggish diffusion reduces dislocation mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice distortions and sluggish diffusion limit thermal expansion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Reduced dislocation mobility and limited thermal expansion provide enhanced mechanical and thermal stability at elevated temperatures.
HfNbTaTiZr will have higher yield strength than pure Nb or a conventional Nb-Ti alloy from 25°C to 1200°C under identical test conditions.
HfNbTaTiZr will have a lower thermal expansion coefficient than pure Nb or a conventional Nb-Ti alloy from 25°C to 1200°C.
HfNbTaTiZr will retain a more stable elastic modulus than pure Nb or a conventional Nb-Ti alloy from 25°C to 1200°C.
The proposed comparison will use uniaxial tensile testing, dilatometry, and elastic-modulus measurements on HfNbTaTiZr and a conventional refractory baseline under identical conditions.
Testing will cover 25°C to 1200°C in an inert atmosphere and use constant tensile strain rates.
The hypothesis is expected to apply at strain rates of approximately 10^-3 to 10^-4 s^-1.
Outside the specified temperature or strain-rate range, phase transformations or oxidation may invalidate the hypothesis.
Failure to observe higher yield strength, lower thermal expansion coefficient, or more stable elastic modulus relative to the baseline across the specified range would falsify the hypothesis.
